results.title: Connecting adb to Lepton (Steamworks Documentation)
results.content:
Android Debug Bridge (ADB) is a tool for communicating with a mobile device from a PC and can be downloaded from Google here. It is also included with Android Studio.  
  
Lepton is a container for running Android apps on Linux devices such as Steam Frame. There is no Lepton container running by default on Steam Frame, so adb will not have anything to connect to until we start one. You can do this by going to your Steam Library on the Steam Frame, find "Lepton Development" and start the application. You should see a floating window appear with an Android home screen.  
  
Note: Launching any Android game from Steam starts a Lepton container and can be connected similarly without needing to launch Lepton Development separately. [...] Note: Your PC likely does not provide enough power over USB to keep the headset running. If you prefer this method you'll want to get a cable or adapter that allows you to connect a separate power source.  
   
Once you have run adb connect you should see:  

connected to frame:5555

  
This means you're successfully connected to the device, and can now deploy builds like you would to any other Android device!

## Troubleshooting

If you get an error, ensure:  

 A Lepton development session is currently running
 The Steam Frame is connected to the same network as your PC
 Your router doesn't have "client isolation" enabled
 You don't have multiple devices on the same network with the same hostname (2 different Steam Frames with the default hostname frame)

results.title: Valve open-sources Lepton, the container that runs Android VR games on Steam Frame
results.content:
Lepton mounts host libraries into the container, including graphics drivers such as mesa and zink, the Steam and Steamworks libraries, and Vulkan layers that Valve names as a "foveated rendering injector" and a "renderpass optimizer". Those two layers are the ones a porting team will care about, because foveated rendering is how a standalone headset buys back the performance it does not have.

The container hooks into strace, gdb, lldb, renderdoc and perfetto, and it hides the flatscreen window by default while letting a developer show it during work. Valve states the purpose in one line: Lepton "is intended to help game developers bring their VR Android games to the Steam Frame".

# Valve open-sources Lepton, the container that runs Android VR games on Steam Frame

Valve open-sources Lepton, the container that runs Android VR games on Steam Frame

Valve has published the source code for Lepton, the Android container that lets Android-only games run on Steam Frame. Valve's README says Lepton "is a tool for use with the Steam client which allows games which are exclusive to Android to run on the Linux operating system".

Steam Frame settings menu inside the headset with the Developer section and the Pair new host button highlighted [...] Valve's Steamworks documentation walks developers through the Frame's developer menu, where the devkit pairing lives. Image: Valve

The frame-public/lepton repository sits on Valve's own GitLab, and its history starts from nothing: the first commit, "Release Lepton v3.0.0", was made by a Valve engineer on September 11 and has no parent. Two release tags follow in the commit log, v3.0.1 dated September 12 and v3.0.2 dated September 17.

## Lepton is a container, not an emulator

The repository splits in two. The image half builds an Android root filesystem, which is the container that games launch inside, and the compat\_tool half is the piece Steam invokes to start a game in that image.

results.title: Valve’s SteamOS stack now covers Windows, x86 and Android on Arm | MLQ News
results.content:
## Lepton brings Android games into Steam’s build system

Lepton is aimed at a separate software ecosystem. Valve describes it as an Android compatibility layer implemented as a container on Linux. That is particularly relevant to Steam Frame because many standalone VR games were first built for Android-based headsets such as Meta Quest. (

Valve’s Steamworks instructions allow a developer to mark Android as a supported operating system, create an Android-specific depot, place an APK in the game files and designate it as the executable. Expansion files can be stored in an obb directory. The Android depot is what allows Steam to install and launch the APK through Lepton. ( [...] # Valve’s SteamOS stack now covers Windows, x86 and Android on Arm

Valve is expanding SteamOS beyond its familiar Proton layer with two additional compatibility technologies for Steam Frame: FEX, which translates x86 software for Arm processors, and Lepton, which runs Android games in a Linux container. Steam Frame is a standalone virtual-reality headset designed primarily to stream a player’s Steam library from a PC, with local support for both VR and non-VR games. ( [...] FEX addresses processor architecture. Steam Frame uses a Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 with an Arm64 instruction set, while most traditional PC games target x86 or x86-64 processors. FEX translates x86 instructions to Arm64 and forwards graphics calls to native host libraries such as Vulkan or OpenGL. Valve also cites code caching as a way to reduce stutter. (

That creates a layered path for many PC games: Proton handles Windows compatibility while FEX handles x86-to-Arm translation. A native Linux ARM64 build can avoid those translation steps, but Valve’s stated preference is to let developers maintain one well-tested version where possible rather than create a lightly supported port.
